title: Software opacity creates attribution traps when harmed outsiders cannot inspect decisive internal state
summary: Candidate pattern opened in rev0011: software can become a hidden witness. When decisive internal state is opaque to patients, operators, subpostmasters, regulators, or the public, early attribution may travel to people or compliant-looking surfaces until a later rail exposes the state mismatch.

status_history.note: Created from Therac-25, Horizon, Dieselgate, and three visibility-rail infrastructure records; explicitly not a mature or universal software theory.

claims.claim: Across Therac-25, Horizon, and Dieselgate, decisive internal software or system state was not readily inspectable by the people most exposed to harm or attribution: patients/operators, subpostmasters, and regulators/public drivers.
what_would_change_status: Counterexamples show harmed outsiders had effective internal-state access or that opacity was incidental rather than structural.

recurring_structure: Decisive internal state is controlled by a complex software/institutional system.
The people or regulators exposed to harm initially see only external symptoms, accounting outputs, compliance results, or operator-console messages.
Attribution can flow toward a person, user, claimant, patient-facing operator, or compliant-looking test result before decisive internal state is visible.
A later visibility rail—engineering analysis, adverse-event reporting, litigation/inquiry, or in-use regulatory testing—creates partial correction memory.
non_equivalences: Therac-25: medical-device safety and interface/interlock failure.
Horizon: software evidence plus legal/institutional denial and disclosure failure.
Dieselgate: deliberate regulatory evasion by state-sensitive software.
MAUDE, Horizon Inquiry, EPA/CARB testing are different infrastructure rails, not interchangeable boards.
maturity_requirements: Add successful-control cases where internal state was inspectable early.
Add source-depth second pass for each child record.
Decide whether pattern should split into medical-device, evidence/legal, and compliance-evasion subpatterns.
type_payload.guardrail: Candidate pattern only; no prevalence estimate, no universal software theory, no claim that opacity alone explains any case.

positive_controls_needed: Add additional records where hidden software state produced external attribution against operators, patients, users, regulators, or the public.
negative_controls_needed: Add records where transparent logs, independent audit access, or adversarial testing prevented misattribution.
counterexamples_to_seek: A software-mediated harm where the decisive internal state was visible and attribution failure was not central.
rollback_triggers: A second-review extraction demotes or materially weakens one of the support records.
A negative-control record shows the pattern label fits too many unrelated cases.
A counterexample shows the claimed recurrence is better explained by a narrower or different mechanism.
The pattern is upgraded only after controls and not by record count alone.
red_team_controls.split_or_merge_watch: High: accidental opacity, institutional denial, intentional evasion, and evidentiary asymmetry should remain separable.

maturity_gate.minimum_before_mature: At least one positive control, at least one negative control, an explicit counterexample search, and a rollback/split decision recorded in the claim-status ledger.

handling_notes: Pattern framing must not erase victims/claimants/patients or become blame theatre.
Keep non-equivalence visible: accidental medical-device harm, wrongful legal attribution, and deliberate regulatory evasion are different kinds of failure.

unknowns: Whether “machine testimony” should become a separate record subtype.
How many software systems have effective internal-state transparency rails.
Whether medical-device, legal-evidence, and compliance-evasion subpatterns should split.
next_actions: Add negative controls and successful-control cases.
Add source-depth second pass for Therac, Horizon, and Dieselgate.
